title: The Power of Habit
author: Charles Duhigg
tagline: Why we do what we do in life and business — and how to change it.

superpower.name: Keystone Habit
superpower.description: One good habit lifts all the others.

overview: Duhigg explains habits through the habit loop of cue, routine and reward, then shows how habits shape organisations and whole societies. The key to change, he argues, is keeping the cue and reward while swapping the routine — and believing change is possible.

chapters.part: Part One · The Habits of Individuals
chapters.title: The Habit Loop
chapters.summary: Habits form when the brain 'chunks' a sequence of actions into an automatic routine to save effort. Every habit follows a loop: a cue that triggers it, a routine that is the behaviour itself, and a reward that tells the brain whether the loop is worth remembering.
keyIdeas: Rewards tell the brain to remember.
chapters.tryThis: Map one habit's cue, routine and reward.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of Duhigg's habit loop?
quiz.explanation: The habit loop drives automatic behaviour.

chapters.part: Part One · The Habits of Individuals
chapters.title: The Craving Brain
chapters.summary: Habits become powerful when they create cravings: the brain begins anticipating the reward as soon as it sees the cue. Marketers used this to create new habits by pairing a clear cue with a satisfying reward and a craving for that reward.
chapters.tryThis: Notice the craving behind one habit you want to change.

quiz.question: What makes a habit powerful according to Duhigg?
quiz.explanation: Anticipation of reward drives the loop.

chapters.part: Part One · The Habits of Individuals
chapters.title: The Golden Rule of Habit Change
chapters.summary: You can't simply eliminate a bad habit, but you can change it: keep the old cue and reward, and insert a new routine. Belief — often found within a group — helps make the change stick through stressful moments.
keyIdeas: Keep cue and reward, change the routine.
chapters.tryThis: For one bad habit, choose a new routine that delivers the same reward.

quiz.question: What is the Golden Rule of Habit Change?
options: Keep cue and reward, change the routine
quiz.explanation: Swapping the routine is the most reliable change.

chapters.part: Part Two · The Habits of Successful Organizations
chapters.title: Keystone Habits
chapters.summary: Some habits matter more than others because they set off chain reactions. Duhigg tells how a focus on worker safety at Alcoa transformed the whole company. Keystone habits create small wins and new structures that spread change.
keyIdeas: Change one key habit to change many.
chapters.tryThis: Pick one keystone habit (like exercise or planning) to focus on.

quiz.question: What is a keystone habit?
options: A habit that triggers widespread change
quiz.explanation: It sets off a cascade of other changes.

chapters.part: Part Two · The Habits of Successful Organizations
chapters.title: Starbucks and the Habit of Success
chapters.summary: Willpower acts like a muscle that can tire but also be strengthened. Starbucks trained staff to plan in advance how they'd react to difficult moments, turning self-control into a habit so it held up under stress.
chapters.tryThis: Write how you'll respond to your next predictable difficult moment.

quiz.question: How did Starbucks strengthen staff willpower?

chapters.part: Part Two · The Habits of Successful Organizations
chapters.title: The Power of a Crisis
chapters.summary: Organisational habits often form as truces between rivals, and poor ones can cause disasters. Good leaders use moments of crisis to reshape institutional habits, because crises make people open to change.
keyIdeas: Crises open the door to change.
chapters.tryThis: Identify a routine at work that persists only because 'that's how it's done'.

quiz.question: Why can crises help leaders?
options: They make people open to changing habits
quiz.explanation: A crisis breaks old truces and routines.

chapters.part: Part Two · The Habits of Successful Organizations
chapters.title: How Target Knows What You Want Before You Do
chapters.summary: Companies analyse purchase data to predict customers' habits and life changes. Duhigg explains that new things are accepted more easily when wrapped in something familiar, so successful products often disguise novelty in old habits.
keyIdeas: Wrap the new in the familiar.
chapters.tryThis: Introduce a new habit by attaching it to something you already enjoy.

quiz.question: What makes new things easier to accept?

chapters.part: Part Three · The Habits of Societies
chapters.title: Saddleback Church and the Montgomery Bus Boycott
chapters.summary: Social movements grow through the habits of friendship, the influence of weak ties in a community and new habits that give people a sense of identity. Duhigg uses the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the growth of Saddleback Church to show how.
chapters.tryThis: Join or start a group that practises a habit you want.

quiz.question: What helps social movements spread according to Duhigg?
options: Friendship, weak ties and new habits

chapters.part: Part Three · The Habits of Societies
chapters.title: The Neurology of Free Will
chapters.summary: If habits run automatically, are we responsible for them? Duhigg argues that once we know a habit exists and how it works, we have the responsibility — and the power — to change it.
chapters.tryThis: Choose one habit you now understand well enough to change, and start.

quiz.question: What does Duhigg conclude about responsibility for habits?
options: Once aware, we're responsible for changing them
quiz.explanation: Knowledge brings the power and duty to change.
